title: How the bishop moves
outcomes: Taps every square a bishop can reach, including captures and blocked diagonals
Says why a bishop can never reach a square of the other colour or a square straight ahead
Frees a boxed-in bishop with a pawn move and reads a bishop move such as Bxf6

steps.caption: A white bishop stands on d4. It moves along four diagonals, each running out to the edge of the board. Every marked square is one it can reach in a single move.

claims.statement: From d4 the bishop reaches exactly 13 squares.

steps.text: A **bishop** moves along a **diagonal**: a line of squares that touch at their corners. In one move it slides as far as it likes along one diagonal, but it stops before its own piece, or lands on an enemy piece and takes it. It cannot jump over a piece. A bishop never moves straight ahead or sideways.

steps.caption: Watch one bishop travel. Each move uses one diagonal, but the next move may use a different one. How far to slide is the player's choice.

line.say: The bishop slides three squares in one move, from d4 all the way to g7.
Black moves the king; this is just a quiet move.
A different diagonal: one square down and to the right, a short slide.
Black waits again.
Now a long slide the other way, five squares along the diagonal, ending on c1.

claims.statement: From d4 the bishop reaches exactly 13 squares.

steps.text: Before you move a bishop, ask three questions. Is the square on one of its diagonals? Is any piece in between? What stands on the square itself? Empty or enemy: allowed, and a capture ends the slide. Your own piece: not allowed. If you are unsure, trace one diagonal at a time on the boards above.

steps.caption: The white pawn on b2 ends that diagonal early: the bishop can stop on c3 but not on b2 or a1, because it cannot land on its own pawn. The black pawn on f6 can be captured, and then the slide ends.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn: the pawn leaves the board and the bishop stops on f6.
Black's king steps aside; the bishop could not have gone on past f6 anyway.

claims.statement: From d4 the bishop reaches exactly 9 squares.

steps.caption: Four diagonals from e3, and each ends differently. Lower left: the edge of the board at c1. Lower right: the white king on g1, so only f2. Upper left: the black knight on c5. Upper right: the white pawn on g5, so only f4.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight and stops on c5; it does not slide on to b6.

claims.statement: From e3 the bishop reaches exactly 6 squares.

steps.caption: A black pawn stands on f6, on the bishop's diagonal, so the bishop may take it. Now imagine that the pawn were White's own. Predict first in the next step, then see the check.

claims.statement: The bishop can capture on f6.

steps.title: Same bishop, one change
steps.prompt: A black pawn stands on f6. Then it becomes White's own pawn. Predict first: can the bishop still go to f6? Then see what a pawn off the diagonal does.

steps.caption: A bishop cannot jump. The black knight on h6 sits on the long diagonal from c1, but White's own pawn on d2 stands in the way. Watch what must happen first.

line.say: The pawn steps aside. Now the diagonal from c1 is clear all the way to h6.
Black does not defend the knight.
The bishop slides five squares and takes the knight.

claims.statement: Right now the bishop cannot go to h6.
After d2-d3 the bishop could capture on h6.

steps.caption: At the start every bishop is boxed in by its own pawns. One pawn step can change that.

line.say: The pawn steps forward and the c1 bishop gets a long open diagonal.
Black does the same on the other side, freeing the bishop on c8.
The bishop slides four squares in one move, to the middle of the board.

claims.statement: At the start the bishop on c1 cannot move.
After the d-pawn steps forward it has 5 squares.
After the black d-pawn moves, the bishop on c8 has 5 squares.

steps.text: **What others said.** Capablanca (*Chess Fundamentals*, sec. 24, as summarised in our reading sheet) treated a bishop shut in behind its own pawns as effectively a piece down, and advised e4 or d4 partly because they free a bishop and the queen. [I] Our reading: a beginner's first bishop job is to give it room.

steps.caption: How a real game often begins. Notice which bishops come out and which stay at home.

line.say: The pawn move opens a diagonal for the bishop on f1 (and for the queen).
Black copies it, opening the diagonal of the bishop on f8.
The bishop slides three squares and now aims at f7, a square it could capture on next.
Black's bishop comes out too, aiming at f2.

claims.statement: After 1.e4 e5 the bishop on f1 has 5 squares.
After 1.e4 e5 the bishop on c1 still cannot move.
After Bc4 the bishop could capture on f7.
After Bc5 the black bishop could capture on f2.

steps.caption: Two bishops, no pawns in the way. The bishop on c1 can reach 7 squares, all dark. The bishop on f1 can reach 7 squares, all light. No square is shared.

line.say: The dark-squared bishop lands on g5, a dark square.
Black makes a quiet move.
The light-squared bishop lands on c4, a light square.

claims.statement: From c1 the bishop reaches exactly 7 squares.
From f1 the bishop reaches exactly 7 squares.

steps.text: Squares are **light** or **dark**, like a chequerboard; a1 is dark. A diagonal step moves one file and one rank, and that always lands on a square of the same colour. So each bishop stays on one colour for the whole game. Your two bishops start on different colours: c1 dark, f1 light. Neither can ever visit the other's squares.

steps.caption: Straight ahead and sideways are never allowed. The pawn on d5 is straight ahead; the pawn on e4 is beside the bishop. The bishop cannot take either one.

claims.statement: The bishop cannot move straight ahead to d5.
The bishop cannot move sideways to e4.
The bishop's destinations are exactly these squares.

steps.caption: A square of the bishop's own colour can still be hard to reach. b8 is dark like d4, but not on any of its diagonals. It takes two moves.

line.say: First move: land on a7, which touches a diagonal of b8.
Black makes a quiet move.
Second move: one step along the new diagonal, and the bishop is on b8.

claims.statement: b8 is not reachable in one move.
Bishop to a7 is legal.
Bishop to e5 is legal.

steps.caption: A bishop in the corner has only one diagonal: the long one, a1 to h8, seven squares. Move the same bishop to the middle and see how its choices grow.

line.say: One slide to the centre, and the bishop has four directions instead of one.

claims.statement: From a1 the bishop reaches exactly 7 squares.
From d4 it reaches 13 squares.

steps.text: **A guess to test.** [H] More squares to choose from usually means more things a bishop can do, so a bishop in the middle should be more useful than one in a corner, and one boxed in by its own pawns least useful of all. What we checked [V]: the counts, 7 and 13. We did not check that more squares wins games.

steps.caption: A bishop attacks every square it could move to, even from far away. The bishop on c3 attacks the pawn on e5, but the pawn on d6 guards it. Taking would cost the bishop for one pawn.

line.say: The bishop captures...
...and the guarding pawn takes it back: a bishop lost for a pawn.

claims.statement: The bishop attacks the pawn on e5.
The pawn on d6 guards e5.
The bishop can capture on e5.

steps.text: **Attack and guard.** A piece guards a square when it could capture there. So a bishop defends its friends and threatens enemies from a distance. Before capturing, ask what guards the target. Teachers often count a bishop as worth about three pawns [R], so giving one for a single pawn is a poor trade.

steps.caption: A bishop can give check along its diagonal. From b5 it looks straight at the king on e8. Black must answer the check.

line.say: Check along the diagonal b5 to e8.
The king steps off the line.

claims.statement: The bishop can move to b5.
After Bb5 the bishop attacks the king on e8.

steps.caption: A knight on d4 reaches 8 squares, none of them in a line. The bishop on d4 reached 13. The knight jumps; the bishop slides.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 reaches exactly 8 squares.

steps.text: **Bishop or knight?** Znosko-Borovsky, as summarised in our reading sheet, held that a knight is weaker than a bishop in open positions and stronger in crowded ones, because it can jump. [H] Our conjecture: a bishop gains most when its diagonals are empty, so before you open the position, ask whether your bishop will gain. Not tested here.
To write a bishop move, use **B** and the square it lands on: *Bg7*. A capture adds an **x**: *Bxf6*. Reading one is just the three questions again: which bishop, which diagonal, which square.
**Teach it.** Imagine a friend who has never played chess. Next you will write down why a bishop stays on one colour and what stops it. A model answer appears after you write.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend who has never played why a bishop that starts on a light square can never visit a dark one, and what stops it sliding through a piece.

steps.text: **A model answer.** Each diagonal step changes file and rank by one, which keeps the square colour, so a bishop stays on its colour. It slides until the next piece: its own piece blocks it, an enemy piece it may take. Compare with yours.
